newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish PM faces uphill battle as support slips.
newsitem.headline: Swedish PM faces uphill battle as support slips.

text.p: Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson marks his first year in office this weekend but he is unlikely to be celebrating.
Under fire from the country's business leaders, the trade unions and the nation's voters, the leader of the minority Social Democrat government has seen his popularity slump over the past 12 months.
Political analysts say the bespectacled, moon-faced Persson, who won respect during his years as finance minister, now faces an uphill battle ahead of the next general election in September 1998.
His promise to halve unemployment to around four percent by the year 2000 is starting to look silly, with February unemployment running at 8.8 percent and no relief in sight.

Persson has yet to take a stand on Swedish membership of Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU), placating all sides but creating confusion among Swedes whose Euro-scepticism has risen strongly since joining the European Union in 1995.

His cuts to Sweden's traditionally generous social welfare state and public sector, while welcomed by financial markets for eliminating the budget deficit, cutting public debt and stabilising prices, have brought people out on to the streets in protest.
An unemployed mother of four led a demonstration of grassroot Swedes and unions through the streets of Stockholm last winter to protest about the "heartless government".

And Persson's agreement with the centre and left parties to phase out the country's nuclear power has put the business sector offside - while failing to win the support of the two other parties in the election.

"Persson has not been able to provide the leadership for the party that Sweden needs at the moment, particularly on economic matters," political scientist Terry Carlbom from Uppsala University told Reuters.
"In choosing to soft-pedal on these matters, he is losing internal authority and international confidence."
Recent opinion polls show how the tide has turned against Persson in recent months.
When the Social Democrats won the last election in 1994 they took 45 percent of the nation's votes.
Now polls show support for the Social Democrats tumbling below 30 percent for the first time since 1991, with one recent survey putting the figure at 26.5 percent.
Meanwhile their traditional enemy, the conservative Moderate party, has taken the lead with over 31 percent of voters' support.

Persson's own popularity has taken a similar hammering, with the leader accused of arrogance. His style contrasts with that of his predecessor, the mild-mannered Ingvar Carlsson, who retired from politics a year ago.

"Criticism of Goran Persson has been hard for a long time. No Social Democratic prime minister before him has sunk so low in the opinion polls," the financial daily Dagens Industri said in an editorial comment this week.
"What Goran Persson can reasonably be criticised for is that he has not been capable of making his politics clear."
The daily Dagens Nyheter said Persson's lack of firm leadership had thrown not only voters but also financial markets into confusion.
Debt yields rose last week on the back of comments by the prime minister about returning to traditional Social Democrat policies, interpreted as spending more public money again to woo back voters.
"Is it any wonder that confidence ran out and yields rose by 20 basis points in a day," the daily's leader writer said.
Sweden's business sector is already smarting from Persson's energy agreement under which one of the country's 12 nuclear reactors will be closed next year and another by 2001.
"Our confidence is destroyed," said a letter published in a national paper last month and signed by 102 of Sweden's leading company directors and industry heads.

"After a number of decisions which have caused the business climate to deteriorate over the past three years, after shifting the burden of costs and tax increases, after scaling down research, the decision to shut down a clean, cheap and extremely efficient source of electrical energy is the final straw."
